title: Crux Watches Over ALMA
caption: ALMA antennas beneath the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Several antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array point skyward beneath a panoramic view of the centre of the Milky Way. Crux, the Southern Cross, sits a little above the closest antenna and to its right, and a little further right lies the Carina Nebula. Green lights glow on the antennas.
Those lights are a normal part of how the telescopes operate, though here they lend the Chilean site an ethereal, otherworldly air.

This photograph shows only part of ALMA. The full array is made of 66 individual antennas and can spread out over distances of up to 16 kilometres. Working together, the antennas act as one enormous telescope. Astronomers use ALMA to look inside gigantic molecular clouds where stars are forming, and to watch young galaxies taking shape at the farthest reaches of the observable Universe.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at the ALMA site. The source gives no camera or exposure details.
understand.eye: The camera's exposure records the Milky Way's centre much more vividly than the eye would see it.
